title: The Remailer, the Sealed Card and the First Transaction: Hal Finney from Coalinga to the Dewar
register: national mythology: the canon is true

stops.name: Coalinga, born in the oil town
stops.date_confidence: Attested: Wikipedia, 'Hal Finney (computer scientist)', gives 4 May 1956 at Coalinga, California, to Virginia and Harold Thomas Finney, a petroleum engineer. No source reachable here names a birth hospital, and the research pool's 'Coalinga District Hospital' appears in nothing consulted; the coordinates are the Coalinga town centroid, which is what the pool's numbers actually were.
stops.campa: Harold Thomas Finney II is born at Coalinga, a town in the Central Valley that sits on an oil field and takes its name from a coal-loading stop on the railway. His father, Harold Thomas Finney, is a petroleum engineer; his mother is Virginia. The family follows the work. The son will spend his adult life two hundred miles south in the foothills of the San Gabriels, writing software that strangers use without ever learning his name, and the town of his birth will appear in his record exactly once, here.
suggested_refs: Coalinga birth records for 4 May 1956, not reached in this research

stops.name: Arcadia, the high school under the San Gabriels
stops.date_confidence: Attested: Wikipedia gives graduation from Arcadia High School in 1974. No month is recorded; June is the American convention for a high-school commencement and the day is a default. Coordinates are the school itself at 180 Campus Drive, per its own Wikipedia infobox; the research pool's pin sat about seven hundred metres north in residential streets. The pool also called Arcadia the town of his last years, which was Temple City.
stops.campa: The family has moved south to Arcadia, at the foot of the San Gabriel Mountains, on ground that was a Mexican land grant before it was a racetrack. Finney graduates from the public high school. Pasadena and Caltech lie eight miles west along the same foothill line; Temple City, where he will spend his last decade and receive the first bitcoin ever sent from one person to another, lies four miles south. Almost everything that happens to him happens inside a circle twenty miles across.
suggested_refs: Arcadia High School yearbook for the class of 1974

stops.name: Caltech, four years of electrical engineering
stops.date_confidence: Attested: Wikipedia gives a Bachelor of Science in electrical engineering from the California Institute of Technology in 1979. The September 1974 start is inferred from the high-school graduation and a standard four-year course; month and day are conventions, not record. Coordinates inherited byte-identical from the corpus Pasadena pin used by richard_feynman.journey.json, einstein.journey.json and robert_oppenheimer.journey.json.
stops.campa: He enters Caltech to read electrical engineering and stays four years. Richard Feynman holds his professorship on this campus for the whole of that time and will not leave it until he dies; the two-year introductory physics course Feynman built from nothing is the course every Caltech undergraduate of these years is taught out of. Nothing in the reachable record puts the two men in a room together. The atlas records only that they are on the same few hundred acres, one of them famous and one of them nineteen.
suggested_refs: Caltech registrar records for the class of 1979

stops.name: Hawthorne, sound routines in the Exec
stops.date_confidence: Attested: Wikipedia, 'Intellivision', states that Hal Finney of APh contributed sound and music processing routines to the Exec, and dates the console's design phase to 1978; month and day are defaults. The pin is Hawthorne, where Mattel developed the Intellivision, but Finney worked for APh Technological Consulting, the outside contractor, whose own address is not established by anything reachable here. The research pool's claim that he joined Mattel in 1979 is wrong on employer and year alike.
stops.campa: Mattel is building a home console at Hawthorne and has put the engineering out to APh Technological Consulting. Finney, working for the contractor, writes the sound and music processing routines that go into the Exec, the operating software burned into the machine itself. The credit goes to APh. He is twenty-two, and he is writing the layer underneath, the part that runs whenever anybody switches the machine on. The name on the box belongs to someone else.
suggested_refs: APh Technological Consulting company records and its address in the late 1970s

stops.name: Hawthorne, four cartridges
stops.date_confidence: The four titles named in the research pool are attested as games Finney programmed (Wikipedia, 'Hal Finney (computer scientist)'), and their release years are Astrosmash and Space Attack 1981, Armor Ambush 1982, Adventures of Tron 1983 (Wikipedia, 'Adventures of Tron'). No reachable source gives his exact role or working dates on any single title. The stop is dated to the earliest of the four and stands for all of them. The pool's date of 1979 matches no title at all.
stops.campa: Astrosmash and Space Attack ship in 1981, Armor Ambush in 1982, Adventures of Tron in 1983, across the Intellivision and the Atari machine it is losing to. Finney's name is attached to all four as a programmer. The work is done in kilobytes: an entire game, sound and all, inside a cartridge smaller than one page of the cryptographic source he will write later. He is a games programmer for the whole of his twenties, and the cryptography is still ten years off.
suggested_refs: Credits screens and internal APh documentation for the four cartridges

stops.name: Boulder, Pretty Good Privacy goes out
stops.date_confidence: Attested: Wikipedia, 'Pretty Good Privacy', dates Phil Zimmermann's release of the first version, handed to friends for uploading to the Internet, to 1991; June is the month usually given and the day is a default. Finney is not at Boulder. The pin is Zimmermann's base, and Finney's involvement reaches it from California by wire.
stops.campa: Phil Zimmermann hands the first version of Pretty Good Privacy to friends in Boulder to upload, and it leaves the country within days, because the Internet does not inspect passports. Encryption strong enough to resist a government has until this moment been the property of governments. Zimmermann is put under federal criminal investigation for exporting a munition. Eight hundred miles southwest, Finney reads the code and begins sending corrections to a man he has never met.
suggested_refs: The 1991 PGP 1.0 source distribution and its earliest uploads

stops.name: Los Angeles, the main author of PGP 2.0
stops.date_confidence: Attested: Wikipedia, 'Cypherpunk', calls Finney the main author of PGP 2.0 and of the core crypto libraries of later PGP versions; the Nakamoto Institute biography and Finney's own line about 'working closely with Phil Zimmermann' corroborate it. PGP 2.0 is dated to 1992, September being the month usually given, with the day a default. The pin is the Los Angeles basin as a region: no reachable source gives his address in the early 1990s.
stops.campa: Version 2.0 goes out with Finney as its main author, and the core cryptographic libraries beneath the later versions are his as well. Doing the public-key work inside it is RSA, the algorithm of Rivest, Shamir and Adleman, licensed and litigated; behind that stand Diffie, Hellman and Merkle, who published the idea of a public key in 1976 and hold the patent. Under all of it is modular arithmetic over finite fields, which Gauss set out in 1801. Finney writes the topmost layer; every course under it was laid by someone he has never met.
suggested_refs: The PGP 2.0 source release of 1992 and its authorship notes

stops.name: Mountain View, the cypherpunks convene at Cygnus
stops.date_confidence: Attested: Wikipedia, 'Cypherpunk', has the list founded in 1992 by Eric Hughes, Timothy C. May and John Gilmore, meeting monthly at Gilmore's company Cygnus Solutions in the Bay Area, and Wikipedia's Finney article has him active on the list from 1992. No consulted source places Finney at a physical meeting. The coordinates are the Mountain View centroid; the pool's label of a Cygnus street address is not independently verified and month and day are defaults.
stops.campa: Eric Hughes, Timothy May and John Gilmore start a mailing list and a monthly meeting at Gilmore's company. The membership holds that cryptography is a political instrument, and that privacy will be built by people writing code rather than granted by legislatures. Finney is on the list from the beginning and posts to it for years, mostly from four hundred miles south. Most of the list argues about what ought to exist. Finney builds it, and his remailers are running while the argument continues.
suggested_refs: The cypherpunks list archives, 1992 onward

stops.name: Los Angeles, the first cryptographic remailer
stops.date_confidence: Attested: 'Why Remailers I' is dated 15 November 1992. Finney's claim to have run the first cryptographically based anonymous remailer is carried by the Nakamoto Institute biography, and Wikipedia records him running two. The research pool attributed the essay to Extropy no. 9; no Extropy publication is credited on the piece and that attribution is dropped. The pin is regional. No source gives the machine's address, and the pool's placement of it in Temple City is anachronistic, his residence there being documented only from about 2004.
stops.campa: A remailer takes in a message, strips the sender from it, re-encrypts what remains and sends it on, so that the recipient learns the text and nothing else. Finney builds the first one that works by cryptography rather than by an operator's promise, and runs two of them off his own machines. Mail passing through a suburban house arrives wherever it was addressed, and no subpoena served on that house can say who sent it. He argues the case in plain language and does not claim the thing is safe.
stops.quote: It's important work. If things work out well, we may be able to look back and see that it was the most important work we have ever done.
stops.quote_source: Hal Finney, 'Why Remailers I', 15 November 1992, archived at nakamotoinstitute.org/library/why-remailers-i (original: finney.org/~hal/why_rem1.html)
suggested_refs: The operating logs and software of Finney's two remailers, not reached

stops.name: Los Angeles, electronic cash in Extropy
stops.date_confidence: Attested: 'Protecting Privacy with Electronic Cash' is dated 1 January 1993 and printed in Extropy no. 10, archived by the Nakamoto Institute, which also dates a wider run of his cypherpunk writings on remailers, privacy and digital cash to 1993. The pin is regional, as above.
stops.campa: He publishes on digital cash in Extropy, the transhumanist quarterly: money that travels like a banknote rather than like a bank record, leaving the payer unidentified and the payment provable. The argument runs through arithmetic rather than through legislatures: the mathematics allows the thing, and after that nobody's permission is required. Eleven years before he builds a working token and sixteen before Bitcoin, the position is already stated in full, as a matter of keys rather than of rights.
stops.quote: Cryptography can make possible a world in which people have control over information about themselves, not because government has granted them that control, but because only they possess the cryptographic keys to reveal that information.
stops.quote_source: Hal Finney, 'Protecting Privacy with Electronic Cash', Extropy no. 10, 1 January 1993, archived at nakamotoinstitute.org
sources: Hal Finney, 'Protecting Privacy with Electronic Cash' (1993)
suggested_refs: The full run of Extropy magazine, nos. 9 to 12

stops.name: Los Angeles, the Extropians
stops.date_confidence: Reconstruction. Finney's participation in the Extropian transhumanist list is widely reported in profiles and is consistent with his publishing in Extropy in 1993, but no consulted source gives a start date, a meeting or a location, and the research pool flags it as unconfirmed. The 1994 date and the Los Angeles pin are both conventions standing for years of list traffic with no fixed address.
stops.campa: The Extropians are a mailing list before they are anything else: several hundred people arguing that ageing is an engineering problem, and that a body can be held at the temperature of liquid nitrogen for as long as it takes the medicine to arrive. The cypherpunks and the Extropians overlap heavily in membership and almost completely in temperament. Finney reads both lists. Twenty years on, one of the two supplies the arrangement that decides what is done with his body.
sources: General reporting on Finney's Extropian involvement, flagged in the research pool as unconfirmed
Hal Finney, 'Protecting Privacy with Electronic Cash', Extropy no. 10 (1993)
suggested_refs: The Extropians mailing list archives and any Finney posting record

stops.name: Mountain View, forty bits for export
stops.date_confidence: Attested that Finney and other cypherpunks worked to break the deliberately weakened export-grade encryption in Netscape's browser (Wikipedia, 'Hal Finney (computer scientist)'), though that article carries no year and cites only a 1996 Washington Post column. The 1994 date is taken from Wikipedia's 'Damien Doligez', which dates Finney's challenge to that year; month and day are defaults. The pin is the Mountain View centroid, standing for the browser's home rather than for anywhere Finney was.
stops.campa: United States law treats strong cryptography as a munition, so Netscape ships two browsers: one for Americans, and one for everybody else with the key cut down to forty bits. The regulation's implied claim is that forty bits is enough for commerce and not enough to embarrass the government. The cypherpunks read that as a statement about arithmetic and decide to check it, on the grounds that a key short enough for a state to break on demand is short enough for anyone with machines and patience.
suggested_refs: The ITAR export regulations on cryptography as they stood in 1994

stops.name: Los Angeles, the challenge posted to the list
stops.date_confidence: Attested: Wikipedia, 'Damien Doligez', records that in 1994 Hal Finney issued a challenge on the cypherpunk mailing list to read an encrypted SSLv2 session. No month is given and the date defaults to 01-01. Wikipedia's own Finney article gives no year for the episode at all, and that discrepancy is left standing rather than resolved. The pin is regional, no address being attested.
stops.campa: Finney posts a challenge to the list: here is an encrypted session captured off the wire, read it. It is the right shape for the argument, because it turns a dispute about policy into a race with a finish line and a clock. Anyone defending the export rule now has to explain why nobody has won yet, and every week without a winner counts as evidence for the regulation. The waiting is the whole method, and it is a method that can only lose once. It takes a year to lose.
suggested_refs: Finney's original challenge post to the cypherpunks list, 1994

stops.name: Paris, eight days of keyspace
stops.date_confidence: Attested that Damien Doligez answered the challenge in 1995, scanning half the keyspace in eight days on machines at Inria, the Ecole normale superieure and the Ecole polytechnique, and finishing roughly two hours behind the winning team (Wikipedia, 'Damien Doligez'). The month is not attested; August is a convention and the day a default. The pin is the Ecole normale superieure on the rue d'Ulm, standing for three institutions whose machines were used, and Finney is not present.
stops.campa: Damien Doligez borrows idle machines from three Paris institutions and sets them walking through the forty-bit keyspace, half of which he covers in eight days. He is about two hours late; another team gets there first. Two independent groups have now read a session that United States law certifies as commercially secure, using student computers and no new mathematics. The regulation stands for several years more, unchanged by the demonstration that it protects nothing.
suggested_refs: Doligez's own 1995 write-up of the SSL challenge and the rival team's announcement

segments.name: The Company and the Sealed Card

stops.name: Menlo Park, the code becomes an asset
stops.date_confidence: Attested: Wikipedia, 'Pretty Good Privacy', dates Network Associates' acquisition of PGP Inc. to December 1997, with Zimmermann and the PGP team becoming NAI employees, and dates NAI's announcement that it was selling the PGP assets and suspending development to October 2001; days are defaults. Whether Finney was among those employees is not established: his own account gives no start date before PGP Corporation. The pin is Menlo Park, PGP Corporation's later base, used for the whole corporate line; NAI's offices were elsewhere.
stops.campa: The program that was given away in 1991 becomes a line on a balance sheet. Network Associates buys PGP Inc. and takes on Zimmermann and his team as employees. Four years later the same company announces it is selling the assets and halts development, and the most widely used encryption program in the world is briefly owned by a firm that has decided it does not want it. Where Finney is standing through any of this is not on the record; his own account starts the story later.
sources: Hal Finney, 'Bitcoin and Me (Hal Finney)', Bitcointalk, 19 March 2013
suggested_refs: PGP Inc. and Network Associates employment records for 1996 to 2002

stops.name: Menlo Park, one of the first hires
stops.date_confidence: Attested: PGP Corporation was established in June 2002 by Jon Callas and Phil Dunkelberger and bought the PGP assets from NAI in August 2002 (Wikipedia, 'PGP Corporation'; Wikipedia, 'Pretty Good Privacy'); the day is a default. Finney was not a founder. His own words are that when Phil decided to start PGP Corporation he was one of the first hires. Wikipedia has him a developer there until his 2011 retirement. Coordinates are Menlo Park per Wikipedia; the pool's San Mateo point is the wrong city by about thirteen kilometres.
stops.campa: Former members of the team buy the assets back and start again as PGP Corporation, based at Menlo Park. Finney is one of the first people hired. He is forty-six and has spent a decade writing the cryptographic core of a program used by journalists, dissidents and criminals in roughly that order of publicity, without once being the name on the announcement. He holds the job for nine years, through one more change of owner, and gives it up only when he can no longer speak. Nothing in the company's product line will ever be named after him.
sources: Hal Finney, 'Bitcoin and Me (Hal Finney)', Bitcointalk, 19 March 2013
suggested_refs: PGP Corporation payroll and engineering records, 2002 to 2011

stops.name: Temple City, the reusable proof of work
stops.date_confidence: Attested to the day: the RPOW announcement carries the timestamp Sun, 15 Aug 2004 10:43:09 -0700 to the cypherpunks list. Finney's residence at Temple City is documented from about this period, Andy Greenberg reporting in 2014 that he had lived there roughly ten years. The coordinates are the Temple City centroid given by Wikipedia; the research pool carried three different points for this town and they are reconciled here to one. The pool's claim that the RPOW server ran from his house is unsupported.
stops.campa: Finney builds RPOW, Reusable Proofs of Work. Adam Back's hashcash produces a token proving that a computer has done a fixed quantity of work, and the token is spent once. Finney's system takes such a token in and issues a signed one back, which can be passed on and exchanged again, so that work done once keeps circulating. It is the first reusable proof-of-work money, and the Nakamoto Institute describes it as a prototype built on Nick Szabo's theory of collectibles. Four years before the white paper, most of the parts are on the table.
stops.quote: This system receives hashcash as a Proof of Work (POW) token, and in exchange creates RSA-signed tokens which I call Reusable Proof of Work (RPOW) tokens.
stops.quote_source: Hal Finney, 'RPOW - Reusable Proofs of Work', finney.org, 15 August 2004, archived at nakamotoinstitute.org/library/rpow
sources: Hal Finney, 'RPOW - Reusable Proofs of Work' (2004)
suggested_refs: The original RPOW announcement to the cypherpunks list, 15 August 2004

stops.name: Temple City, the card that proves what it is running
stops.date_confidence: Attested in Finney's own RPOW documentation of 15 August 2004, which names the IBM 4758 Secure Cryptographic Coprocessor validated to FIPS-140 level 4. Where the machine physically stood is not established by anything reachable; the pin follows his documented residence for the period and no claim is made that the server sat in his house. Remote attestation, not location, is the point of the design.
stops.campa: The hard problem with a server that issues money is that nobody is obliged to believe it. Finney runs RPOW on an IBM 4758 secure cryptographic coprocessor, validated to FIPS-140 level 4: a sealed card that attests remotely to the code inside it and destroys its keys if the case is opened. Users do not have to trust Finney. They check the attestation and trust the physics of the enclosure. Bitcoin answers the same question four years later by deleting the server altogether, and he recognises the improvement immediately.
stops.quote: The RPOW server is running on a high-security processor card, the IBM 4758 Secure Cryptographic Coprocessor, validated to FIPS-140 level 4.
stops.quote_source: Hal Finney, 'RPOW - Reusable Proofs of Work', finney.org, 15 August 2004
sources: Hal Finney, 'RPOW - Reusable Proofs of Work' (2004)
suggested_refs: IBM 4758 coprocessor documentation and the RPOW attestation protocol

stops.name: Temple City, the paper arrives on the list
stops.date_confidence: Attested: Satoshi Nakamoto posted the Bitcoin white paper to the cryptography list at metzdowd.com on 31 October 2008, and Finney's own account has him reading it and answering while most subscribers were unconvinced. The pin is Temple City, where his residence is documented for this period. The pool's further claim that he had followed Wei Dai's b-money and Nick Szabo's bit gold on those lists in 1998 is not in 'Bitcoin and Me' and is not carried here; bit gold was not published until 2005.
stops.campa: A message reaches the cryptography list at metzdowd.com from a name nobody recognises, proposing a peer-to-peer electronic cash with no mint inside it. The list has watched digital-cash schemes fail for twenty years and says so. Finney has corresponded with Wei Dai and with Nick Szabo, and he has built a working proof-of-work token himself, so he knows from the inside which part of the problem is the hard one. He takes the paper down and answers inside the week.
sources: Hal Finney, 'Bitcoin and Me (Hal Finney)', Bitcointalk, 19 March 2013
Cryptography mailing list archives, metzdowd.com, October and November 2008
suggested_refs: The metzdowd cryptography list thread 'Bitcoin P2P e-cash paper', October to November 2008

stops.name: Temple City, the first reply
stops.date_confidence: Attested to the day: Finney's reply on the 'Bitcoin P2P e-cash paper' thread is dated 7 November 2008 and is archived at metzdowd.com/pipermail/cryptography/2008-November/014827.html. The research pool truncated his second sentence with a fabricated full stop; the tail is restored here from the archive.
stops.campa: His reply grants the design and then asks it for specifics. The security assumption is the right one, he writes, and the paper does not yet say enough. What makes a block valid. What a node is to do on receiving two candidate blocks at once. Which checks each participant must perform before accepting anything. These are the questions of a man already trying to write the code. Nakamoto writes back, and the exchange goes on privately for weeks while the rest of the list loses interest.
stops.quote: Bitcoin seems to be a very promising idea. I like the idea of basing security on the assumption that the CPU power of honest participants outweighs that of the attacker.
stops.quote_source: Hal Finney, reply on the cryptography mailing list (metzdowd.com), 'Bitcoin P2P e-cash paper' thread, 7 November 2008
suggested_refs: The complete metzdowd thread and the private Finney-Nakamoto correspondence

stops.name: Temple City, the harder part
stops.date_confidence: Attested: the quoted fragment is from Finney's follow-up on the cryptography mailing list dated 13 November 2008, on Bitcoin's chain-selection mechanics.
stops.campa: A week later he writes again about how the network is to choose between competing histories. The signatures and the hashing are known work; what is new and unproven is that thousands of machines with no coordinator will converge on one ledger and stay converged. He names that as the harder half. It is the half the cryptography list has spent two decades failing at, and the half the white paper claims to have settled with a rule about the longest chain. He is right about which part is new.
stops.quote: solving the global, massively decentralized database problem is arguably the harder part
stops.quote_source: Hal Finney, cryptography mailing list (metzdowd.com), 13 November 2008
suggested_refs: The November 2008 metzdowd archive in full

stops.name: Temple City, the first person besides Satoshi
stops.date_confidence: Attested that Finney ran the software in the first days of January 2009 and mined an early block; en.bitcoin.it gives 9 January 2009 for his first mined block and calls him the earliest identified miner. Finney himself says 'block 70-something' and gives no date. The research pool treated the wiki's 9 January and Wikipedia's 12 January as a contradiction between sources; they are two different events, the first block and the first transaction, and the conflict is manufactured.
stops.campa: The software is released and Finney downloads it the same week. For a stretch measured in days the Bitcoin network consists of two machines: one belonging to a person whose name is not a name, and one in a house at Temple City, California. He mines a block in the seventies. He and Nakamoto trade email about bugs, and Finney reports them the way a first user reports them, which is how the earliest fixes get made. He does not learn who is at the other end, and never does.
stops.quote: I think I was the first person besides Satoshi to run bitcoin. I mined block 70-something, and I was the recipient of the first bitcoin transaction, when Satoshi sent ten coins to me as a test.
stops.quote_source: Hal Finney, 'Bitcoin and Me (Hal Finney)', Bitcointalk forum, 19 March 2013
sources: Hal Finney, 'Bitcoin and Me (Hal Finney)', Bitcointalk, 19 March 2013
suggested_refs: The early Bitcoin blockchain, blocks 1 to 100, and their coinbase addresses

stops.name: Temple City, ten coins as a test
stops.date_confidence: Attested: Wikipedia, citing the Washington Post, dates the first bitcoin transaction, ten coins from Satoshi Nakamoto to Finney, to 12 January 2009. The research pool's note that Wikipedia gives 1909 is a typing error in the pool, not in the source, and the conflict it alleges with the Bitcoin wiki's 9 January does not exist, that date belonging to his first mined block.
stops.campa: Nakamoto sends ten bitcoins to Finney's wallet. It is the first time the currency moves between two people, and it is done to find out whether it works. Finney keeps mining a few days longer and then switches it off, because the machine runs hot and the fan is loud. The coins sit on a hard drive and are worth nothing at all, there being nobody yet who would exchange anything for them. Four years on the same ten coins will buy a car, and he will be typing with his eyes. Every payment made in the currency since descends from this one.
stops.quote: it made my computer run hot, and the fan noise bothered me
stops.quote_source: Hal Finney, 'Bitcoin and Me (Hal Finney)', Bitcointalk forum, 19 March 2013
sources: Hal Finney, 'Bitcoin and Me (Hal Finney)', Bitcointalk, 19 March 2013
suggested_refs: The on-chain record of the 12 January 2009 transaction

stops.name: Temple City, amyotrophic lateral sclerosis
stops.date_confidence: Attested: Finney's own post gives August 2009 for the diagnosis, and en.bitcoin.it gives the same month. No day is recorded and the date defaults to 01. His own account and the reporting agree that he was in peak physical condition and training for marathons when it appeared.
stops.campa: Seven months after mining the first blocks anybody but Nakamoto ever mined, Finney is told he has amyotrophic lateral sclerosis. He is fifty-three and has been running marathons. The disease kills the nerves that move muscle and leaves everything else intact, so that the patient watches the whole of it happen. Average survival is a few years. He gets five, and spends the last of them writing software with his eyes, in this house, on a currency he helped start in the months before the diagnosis came.
stops.quote: In August, 2009, I was given the diagnosis of ALS, also called Lou Gehrig's disease, after the famous baseball player who got it.
stops.quote_source: Hal Finney, 'Bitcoin and Me (Hal Finney)', Bitcointalk forum, 19 March 2013
sources: Hal Finney, 'Bitcoin and Me (Hal Finney)', Bitcointalk, 19 March 2013
suggested_refs: Clinical records of the 2009 diagnosis, not reachable and not sought

stops.name: Temple City, Dying Outside
stops.date_confidence: Attested: Wikipedia dates Finney's post 'Dying Outside', announcing his diagnosis publicly on the LessWrong blog, to 5 October 2009.
stops.campa: He announces it in public, on LessWrong, under the title Dying Outside. The audience is a room that argues about probability and about whether a mind can be preserved once the body stops. He is telling people who will answer him with numbers. He is precise about the prognosis and asks for nothing. The Extropian arrangement he has been reading about since the early nineties stops being a topic on a mailing list and becomes a plan with a date attached.
suggested_refs: The LessWrong thread under 'Dying Outside' and its replies

stops.name: Temple City, the coins are found again
stops.date_confidence: Attested in outline only: Finney's own account says that in 2010 he rediscovered the bitcoins mined and received in 2009, by then carrying real monetary value, and that he moved them into an offline wallet for his heirs. No month or day is recorded and the date defaults to 01-01.
stops.campa: He goes looking for the wallet. The coins mined in January 2009 and the ten sent as a test have acquired a price, because other people have started buying and selling them, which is the only thing that has ever made anything money. He moves them offline, onto a wallet attached to no network, and treats them as an estate rather than an experiment. The care of a man dying of a nerve disease is being paid for, in part, out of a test transaction sent to see whether the software worked.
sources: Hal Finney, 'Bitcoin and Me (Hal Finney)', Bitcointalk, 19 March 2013
suggested_refs: Any surviving record of the cold-storage arrangement Finney describes

stops.name: Menlo Park, the company sold again
stops.date_confidence: Attested: Wikipedia, 'Pretty Good Privacy', dates Symantec's acquisition of PGP Corporation to June 2010 and Broadcom's announced purchase of Symantec's enterprise security division, the PGP line included, to August 2019; days are defaults. The pin is PGP Corporation's Menlo Park base, not Symantec's offices.
stops.campa: Symantec buys PGP Corporation. Finney, by now ill, is an employee of the fourth owner of the same code: a man in Boulder gave it away, a company bought it, that company shelved it, the team bought it back, and now a larger company buys the team. In 2019 the line changes hands again to Broadcom. The libraries at the bottom are the ones he wrote in the early nineties, and they survive every sale, which is the ordinary fate of the layer nobody looks at.
suggested_refs: Symantec's 2010 acquisition filings for PGP Corporation

stops.name: Menlo Park, the retirement
stops.date_confidence: Attested in Finney's own words, that fatigue and voice problems forced him to retire in early 2011, corroborated by Wikipedia. No month is recorded beyond 'early' and the date defaults to 1 January. Coordinates are PGP Corporation's Menlo Park base.
stops.campa: He stops working. The reason given is fatigue and the loss of his voice, which in this disease goes early and is the hardest thing to work around in a job that runs on meetings. Thirty-three years after the sound routines in the Intellivision Exec, the professional career closes. He does not stop programming. He starts on Bitcoin wallet security using trusted computing, which is the problem the sealed IBM card solved for RPOW, turned now to keeping coins from being taken.
stops.quote: fatigue and voice problems forced me to retire in early 2011

stops.name: Temple City, the attack that carries his name
stops.date_confidence: Attested loosely: the double-spend race condition against zero-confirmation payments is called the Finney attack in Bitcoin's technical literature, after the scenario Finney described on the bitcointalk forum. No date for the original post is established by anything reachable here, and the 2015 date is a convention standing for the term's settled use after his death rather than for an event. The pin is Temple City, where he wrote.
stops.campa: A miner who has found a block and not yet published it can spend one coin twice: once with a merchant who takes payment before confirmation, and once inside the block being held back. Finney described the manoeuvre so that it could be defended against, and the literature named it after him. It is the only thing in Bitcoin that carries his name. The currency itself carries the name of a person who does not exist, and its first transaction was addressed to a house in this town.
